write.desc: This topic studies two global properties of subsets of the real line: connectedness, which turns out to mean being an interval and is the reason behind the intermediate value theorem, and perfectness, with the Cantor set as the standard example of a set that is uncountable yet has total length zero and contains no interval; it ends by noting that all these ideas carry over to metric spaces.

points.name: Separated sets and connected sets
points.what: The learner can state when two sets are separated (neither meets the closure of the other) and when a set is connected (it is not the union of two nonempty separated sets). They can prove that Q, and a union of two disjoint intervals such as (0,1) ∪ (2,3), are disconnected, and explain why (0,1) ∪ (1,2) is disconnected while [0,1) ∪ [1,2) is not a separation.
outside: closure of a set (A together with its limit points)

points.name: Connected subsets of R are exactly the intervals
points.what: The learner can prove that a subset E of R is connected exactly when it has the interval property (if a < c < b with a, b in E, then c is in E), using the supremum of the part of a separation lying below a chosen point. They can explain that this theorem is what the intermediate value theorem rests on.
outside: least upper bound property (completeness axiom) of R
closure of a set (A together with its limit points)

points.name: Perfect sets
points.what: The learner can define a perfect set as a closed set with no isolated points and decide for given examples, such as [a,b], R, finite sets, Z and {0} ∪ {1/n}, whether they are perfect, justifying each answer from the definitions.
outside: closed sets defined as sets containing all their limit points
isolated points and limit points of a set

points.name: Nonempty perfect sets are uncountable
points.what: The learner can follow and reproduce the proof that a nonempty perfect set P is uncountable: assuming P = {x1, x2, ...}, build a decreasing sequence of nonempty compact sets (closed intervals intersected with P) each avoiding x_n, and use the nested compact set property to reach a contradiction.
outside: nested compact set property (decreasing nonempty compact sets have nonempty intersection)
Heine-Borel theorem (closed and bounded sets are compact)

points.name: Constructing the Cantor set
points.what: The learner can describe the Cantor set as the intersection of the sets C_n obtained by repeatedly removing open middle thirds, prove it is closed, bounded and therefore compact, show it is nonempty (it contains 0, 1 and all endpoints), and use a geometric series to show the removed intervals have total length 1.
outside: arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed
Heine-Borel theorem (closed and bounded sets are compact)

points.name: The Cantor set is perfect and uncountable
points.what: The learner can prove that every point of the Cantor set is a limit of endpoints of the C_n, so the set is perfect, and can show it is uncountable in two ways: by the perfect set theorem, and by matching its points with ternary expansions using only the digits 0 and 2 and comparing with infinite binary sequences.
outside: uncountability of the set of infinite binary sequences (Cantor diagonal argument)
decimal-style expansions of real numbers in a base

points.name: The Cantor set contains no interval and is totally disconnected
points.what: The learner can prove that the Cantor set contains no interval of positive length, because C_n has total length (2/3)^n, and deduce from the intervals theorem that its only connected subsets are single points. They can use the Cantor set to explain why 'uncountable' and 'large in length' are different notions of size.

points.name: Looking ahead: these ideas in metric spaces
points.what: The learner can explain that neighbourhoods, open and closed sets, compactness and connectedness are defined using only the distance |x - y|, so they make sense in any metric space, and that there closed and bounded no longer implies compact (for example, an infinite set with the discrete metric).
outside: open and closed sets defined via epsilon-neighbourhoods
Heine-Borel theorem (closed and bounded sets are compact)

where.title: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd ed.)

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis
